summary: Mathematical reasoning demands two critical, complementary skills: constructing rigorous proofs for true statements and discovering counterexamples that disprove false ones. However, current AI efforts in mathematics focus almost exclusively on proof construction, often neglecting the equally important task of finding counterexamples. In this paper, we address this gap by fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to reason about and generate counterexamples. We formalize this task as formal counterexample generation, which requires LLMs not only to propose candidate counterexamples but also to produce formal proofs that can be automatically verified in the Lean 4 theorem prover. To enable effective learning, we introduce a symbolic mutation strategy that constructs candidate counterexample-generation tasks by systematically extracting theorems and removing selected hypotheses. Together with curated datasets, this strategy enables a multi-reward expert iteration framework that substantially enhances both the effectiveness and efficiency of training LLMs for counterexample generation and theorem proving. Experiments on three newly collected benchmarks validate the advantages of our approach, showing that the mutation strategy and training framework yield substantial performance gains.

summary: Hydrogen threatens the structural integrity of metals and thus predicting hydrogen-material interactions is key to unlocking the role of hydrogen in the energy transition. Quantifying the interplay between material deformation and hydrogen diffusion ahead of cracks and other stress concentrators is key to the prediction and prevention of hydrogen-assisted failures. In this work, a generalised theoretical and computational framework is presented that for the first time encompasses: (i) stress-assisted diffusion, (ii) hydrogen trapping due to multiple trap types, rigorously accounting for the rate of creation of dislocation trap sites, (iii) hydrogen transport through dislocations, (iv) equilibrium (Oriani) and non-equilibrium (McNabb-Foster) trapping kinetics, (v) hydrogen-induced softening, and (vi) hydrogen uptake, considering the role of hydrostatic stresses and local electrochemistry. Particular emphasis is placed on the numerical implementation in COMSOL Multiphysics, releasing the relevant models and discussing stability, discretisation and solver details. Each of the elements of the framework is independently benchmarked against results from the literature and implications for the prediction of hydrogen-assisted fractures are discussed. The second part of this work (Part II) shows how these crack tip predictions can be combined with crack growth simulations.

summary: We study the performance of sequential contention resolution and matching algorithms on random graphs with vanishing edge probabilities. When the edges of the graph are processed in an adversarially-chosen order, we derive a new OCRS that is $0.382$-selectable, attaining the "independence benchmark" from the literature under the vanishing edge probabilities assumption. Complementary to this positive result, we show that no OCRS can be more than $0.390$-selectable, significantly improving upon the upper bound of $0.428$ from the literature. We also derive negative results that are specialized to bipartite graphs or subfamilies of OCRSs. Meanwhile, when the edges of the graph are processed in a uniformly random order, we show that the simple greedy contention resolution scheme which accepts all active and feasible edges is $1/2$-selectable. This result is tight due to a known upper bound. We then show that when the algorithm can choose the processing order, a slight tweak to the random order---give each vertex a random priority and process edges in lexicographic order---results in a strictly better contention resolution scheme that is $1-\ln(2-1/e)\approx0.510$-selectable. Moreover, we show that this bound is tight over any sequential contention resolution scheme, even one which may adaptively choose the order in which it processes edges. This provides a separation from the $0.544$ upper bound for offline contention resolution implied by the classic result of Karp and Sipser. Our positive results also apply to online matching on $1$-uniform random graphs with vanishing (non-identical) edge probabilities, extending and unifying some results from the random graphs literature.

summary: We introduce an automated, formal, counterexample-based approach to synthesise Barrier Certificates (BC) for the safety verification of continuous and hybrid dynamical models. The approach is underpinned by an inductive framework: this is structured as a sequential loop between a learner, which manipulates a candidate BC structured as a neural network, and a sound verifier, which either certifies the candidate's validity or generates counter-examples to further guide the learner. summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 42 examines why enterprise artificial intelligence strategy is moving beyond the assumption that one general-purpose model should serve every workload. The paper argues that model selection is increasingly an intelligence-allocation decision involving capability, cost, latency, governance, data restrictions, decision authority and measurable business outcomes. As enterprise AI expands across routine classification, specialised extraction, complex reasoning, multimodal production and consequential decisions, different categories of work require different execution approaches. The paper distinguishes model selection, inference tiering, model routing, policy-controlled routing and outcome verification. It proposes that enterprises should first determine whether generative inference is required, define the minimum capability needed, apply mandatory eligibility constraints, select an appropriate execution route, establish escalation conditions and verify whether the completed outcome meets a predetermined business acceptance standard. Six author-developed frameworks structure this operating model. The AI Workload Classification framework divides work into deterministic, routine language, specialised, complex reasoning and consequential-decision categories. The Model Routing Matrix separates mandatory policy constraints from economic and performance preferences. The Capability-Cost Frontier evaluates eligible models against verified acceptance and complete delivery cost. The Model Escalation Ladder defines structured movement from deterministic execution through compact, specialised and frontier intelligence to human authority. Minimum Sufficient Intelligence identifies the least expensive eligible intelligence capable of satisfying the complete business requirement. Cost per Accepted Outcome, or CPAO, measures total attributable workflow delivery cost against completed business outcomes that satisfy defined acceptance standards. The analysis also challenges the assumption that sophisticated routing automatically produces superior economics. Evidence from LLMRouterBench shows strong model complementarity while demonstrating that several routing approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines. The paper therefore argues that routing complexity requires evidence of incremental value rather than being treated as an architectural objective in itself. Commercial case studies examine three different intelligence-allocation mechanisms. Sword Health illustrates central gateway control, provider portability, policy enforcement and cost attribution. Forethought demonstrates how specialised deployment, multi-model endpoints and serverless inference affect AI infrastructure economics. gimmefy illustrates multimodel execution across different marketing modalities and provider capabilities. The cases are treated separately because their reported outcomes rely on different commercial baselines and measurement approaches. The paper proposes a 90-day evaluation path based on workload classification, baseline measurement, shadow testing, controlled deployment and an explicit investment decision. Leadership measurement should focus on accepted outcome rate, cost per accepted outcome, realised business value, consequential errors, latency distribution, policy compliance, escalation and rework, and model substitution readiness. The central argument is that enterprise advantage will come from disciplined allocation of intelligence rather than maximising model capability or model count. The appropriate question is which intelligence should handle each workload, under what authority, and at what verified cost of successful execution. The AI Workload Classification framework, Model Routing Matrix, Capability-Cost Frontier, Model Escalation Ladder, Minimum Sufficient Intelligence principle and Cost per Accepted Outcome framework are author-developed analytical constructs. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. The discussion of the Almoravids emphasises their origins among Saharan Berber communities associated with territories situated in present-day Mauritania, thereby questioning the assumption that their subsequent expansion establishes a uniquely Moroccan historical entitlement.
